questions.question: A 30-year-old athlete complains of difficulty in flexion at the metatarsophalangeal joint and extension at the interphalangeal joint of the second toe. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.A: First lumbrical is affected and is supplied by the lateral plantar nerve.
options.B: First lumbrical is affected and is supplied by the medial plantar nerve.
options.C: Second lumbrical is affected and is supplied by the lateral plantar nerve.
options.D: Second lumbrical is affected and is supplied by the medial plantar nerve.

explanation.text: The first lumbrical, which acts on the second toe, is supplied by the medial plantar nerve. It facilitates flexion at the metatarsophalangeal joint and extension at the interphalangeal joints. The lumbricals of the foot show a pattern of dual innervation: The medial plantar nerve innervates the first lumbrical. The second, third, and fourth lumbricals are innervated by the lateral plantar nerve.
This distribution mirrors the innervation seen in the hand, where a division between median and ulnar nerve innervation exists.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man presents with complaints of claudication and cramping pain in his left lower limb while walking short distances, which is relieved by rest. On further examination, his left dorsalis pedis pulse is diminished, and he has cool skin on the affected leg. Doppler ultrasound reveals significant atherosclerosis at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery. Which of the following arteries, if most affected by this condition, is likely responsible for the reduced blood flow to his lower limb?

explanation.text: External iliac artery is the primary artery that continues as the femoral artery to supply the lower limb. Atherosclerosis at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery directly affects the external iliac artery, reducing blood flow to the entire lower limb, causing claudication. The internal iliac artery primarily supplies the pelvis and perineum.

The internal pudendal artery a branch of the internal iliac artery, supplies the genitalia and perineum, not the lower limb. The inferior epigastric artery, a branch of the external iliac artery, supplies the anterior abdominal wall, not the lower limb. Reference:

questions.question: During surgery for a femoral shaft fracture, the surgeon notes damage to the vastus lateralis muscle. Which artery is primarily responsible for supplying the vastus lateralis?

options.A: Ascending branch of femoral circumflex artery
options.B: Ascending branch of medial femoral circumflex artery
options.C: Descending branch of lateral femoral circumflex artery
options.D: Transverse branch if medial femoral circumflex artery

explanation.text: The descending branch of the lateral femoral circumflex artery supplies the vastus lateralis muscle as it descends along its anterior border.

Medial and Lateral Femoral Circumflex Arteries Branches of the profunda femoris artery (from the femoral artery) Main blood supply to adductor, extensor, and flexor thigh muscles Anastomose with internal/external iliac arteries (superior) and popliteal artery (inferior) Lateral Femoral Circumflex Artery Branches near the root of profunda femoris, run laterally Divides into ascending, descending, and transverse branches Branches: Branch Course Function/Anastomosis Ascending (Option A) Ascends along intertrochanteric line, under tensor fasciae latae Supplies greater trochanter, forms anastomotic ring around femoral neck (with medial femoral circumflex artery) Descending (Option C) Descends posterior to rectus femoris, along anterior vastus lateralis Supplies vastus lateralis, anastomoses with superior lateral genicular artery (at knee) Transverse Passes laterally, anterior to vastus intermedius, pierces vastus lateralis near greater trochanter Forms cruciate anastomosis (with medial femoral circumflex, inferior gluteal, and first perforating arteries) Medial Femoral Circumflex Artery Typically branches from profunda femoris, sometimes from the femoral artery Supplies adductor muscles, runs medially around femur Branches: Branch Course Function/Anastomosis Transverse (Option D) Runs near quadratus femoris Contributes to cruciate anastomosis Ascending (Option B) Ascends on obturator externus tendon, reaches trochanteric fossa Anastomoses with gluteal and lateral femoral circumflex arteries, supplies hip joint via the acetabular branch.

Anastomoses: Anastomosis Location Involved Arteries Trochanteric anastomosis Trochanteric fossa Ascending branch of medial femoral circumflex, superior/inferior gluteal arteries, lateral femoral circumflex, first perforating artery Cruciate anastomosis Lesser trochanter (inferior) Transverse branches of medial and lateral femoral circumflex, inferior gluteal artery, first perforating artery

questions.question: A patient is experiencing discomfort in the lower limb due to venous insufficiency. Which of the following mechanisms aid in the venous return of blood from the lower limb to the heart?

options.B: Contraction of calf muscles leads to compression of superficial veins

explanation.text: The deep fascia enhances the muscle pump by limiting outward muscle expansion, helping direct blood flow upwards through deep veins. Venous Drainage of the Lower Limb The venous system of the lower limb returns deoxygenated blood to the heart. Key aspects include vein groups, connections, and clinical significance. Groups of Veins Superficial Veins: Located in subcutaneous tissue, above the deep fascia.

Deep Veins: Positioned deep to the fascia, accompany major arteries, and are more numerous than superficial veins. Important Superficial Veins Vein Type Description Great Saphenous Longest vein in the body; originates on the medial foot, ascends along the medial leg and thigh to the femoral vein; significant for venous return and surgical grafts.

Small Saphenous Originates on the lateral foot, ascends posteriorly along the leg, drains into the popliteal vein in the fossa. Perforating Veins Connect superficial and deep venous systems. Contain valves for unidirectional blood flow, preventing backflow. Factors Aiding Venous Return Valves: Ensure unidirectional flow towards the heart.

Muscle Pump: Calf muscle contraction compresses deep veins, aiding blood propulsion. (Option B) Deep Fascia: Limits muscle expansion, enhancing pressure on deep veins during contraction. (Option A) Negative Intrathoracic Pressure: Assists in drawing blood upwards during inspiration. (Option C) Clinical Significance: Varicose Veins Definition: Enlarged, twisted veins caused by incompetent valves allowing backward blood flow, leading to dilation.

Contributing Factors: Malfunctioning valves, causing blood to backflow, pool, and lead to dilation. Incompetent perforating veins allow high-pressure deep blood to flow into the superficial system, exacerbating varicosity.
**Vasodilation of superficial veins (Option D):** Vasodilation would increase venous pressure and contribute to venous insufficiency, not aid in venous return.

questions.question: A 30-year-old female presents to the emergency department with a swollen right leg and pain following a long-haul flight. Doppler ultrasound confirms a deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in the right calf. Which statement about the anatomy of the deep veins of the lower limb is correct?

options.A: The anterior tibial vein runs alongside the fibular artery.
options.B: The medial and lateral plantar veins contribute to the formation of the popliteal vein.
options.C: Perforating veins carry blood from deep veins to superficial veins.
options.D: The fibular veins drain directly into the femoral vein.

explanation.text: The medial and lateral plantar veins unite to form the posterior tibial veins, which then contribute to the formation of the popliteal vein. Deep Veins of the Lower Limb Deep veins are located beneath the deep fascia of the lower limb, running alongside major arteries and are more numerous than superficial veins. They generally share names with their accompanying arteries and follow similar paths.

Characteristics: Feature Description Connections Receive blood from superficial veins via perforating veins equipped with valves for unidirectional flow. Venous Return Role Critical for returning blood to the heart; compression during muscle contraction (especially calf muscles) propels blood upward (muscle pump). Clinical Significance Important in conditions like Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) and potential complications such as pulmonary embolism.

Specific Deep Veins: Vein Description Plantar Digital Veins Originate in toes, contributing to plantar metatarsal veins. Plantar Metatarsal Veins Run in intermetatarsal spaces, connecting with dorsal veins via perforating veins. Deep Plantar Venous Arch Formed by plantar metatarsal veins; gives rise to medial and lateral plantar veins. Medial & Lateral Plantar Veins Course alongside corresponding arteries; contribute to posterior tibial veins.

They contribute to the formation of the popliteal vein. (Option B) Posterior Tibial Veins Formed behind the medial malleolus by the union of medial and lateral plantar veins. Anterior Tibial Veins Accompany the anterior tibial artery. Fibular Veins Run alongside the fibular artery. Popliteal Vein Formed by the union of anterior and posterior tibial veins and the fibular vein; ascends to become femoral vein.

Femoral Vein Main deep vein of the thigh; receives blood from popliteal vein, profunda femoris vein, and long saphenous vein. Profunda Femoris Vein Drains deep structures of the thigh; merges with the femoral vein. Conditions: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT): Formation of a thrombus in deep veins, often in the calf due to sluggish blood flow.
Pulmonary Embolism: Thrombus fragments can dislodge, travel to the lungs, and cause a life-threatening blockage.
**The anterior tibial vein runs alongside the fibular artery (Option A):** The anterior tibial vein runs alongside the anterior tibial artery.

**Perforating veins carry blood from deep veins to superficial veins (Option C):** Perforating veins allow blood to flow from superficial veins to deep veins. The fibular veins drain directly into the femoral vein. (Option D): The fibular veins drain into the popliteal vein, not directly into the femoral vein.

questions.question: A 35-year-old female presents with symptoms of heaviness and visible varicose veins primarily affecting her left leg. Duplex ultrasonography reveals dilation of the great saphenous vein (GSV) with incompetent valves. She is scheduled for vein stripping surgery. Which of the following statements regarding the anatomical features of the GSV compared to the small saphenous vein (SSV) is correct?

options.A: The GSV has fewer valves than the SSV, making it less prone to varicosities
options.B: The GSV originates from the lateral end of the dorsal venous arch of the foot
options.C: The GSV is a continuation of the medial marginal vein.
options.D: The GSV pierces the deep fascia to drain into the popliteal vein.

explanation.text: The GSV arises from the medial marginal vein on the dorsum of the foot.

Superficial Veins of the Lower Limb Superficial veins are located in the subcutaneous tissue, above the deep fascia They drain blood from superficial lower limb tissues Important superficial veins: Great Saphenous Vein (GSV) and Small Saphenous Vein (SSV) Great Saphenous Vein (GSV) Feature Description Origin Arises on the dorsum of the foot, as a continuation of the medial marginal vein (Option C) Course Ascends in front of the medial malleolus Runs along the medial leg Courses behind the knee Inclines forward in the thigh Passes through the saphenous opening into the femoral vein Tributaries Dorsal venous arch of the foot Medial marginal vein Posterior arch vein Calf vein Accessory saphenous vein Anterior cutaneous vein of the thigh Superficial epigastric, circumflex iliac, and external pudendal veins Valves Contains 10-20 valves, more concentrated in the leg (Option A) Clinical Significance Commonly used in surgical grafting, especially for coronary artery bypass Small Saphenous Vein (SSV) Feature Description Origin Forms on the dorsum of the foot from the lateral dorsal venous arch (Option B) Course Ascends behind the lateral malleolus Runs along the calf Drains into the popliteal vein after piercing the deep fascia (Option D) Tributaries Receives cutaneous tributaries from the lateral foot, heel, and back of the leg Connections Communicates with deep veins and connects with GSV through branches Valves Contains 7-13 valves, with one near its termination Termination Variability May join GSV, bifurcate, or drain into other veins Clinical Relevance Varicose Veins: Dilated, tortuous veins due to valve incompetence, commonly in GSV and tributaries Venous Return: Superficial veins aid blood return to the heart via muscle pump mechanism, facilitated by valves in perforating veins

questions.question: A 45-year-old female presents with burning pain and tingling in the plantar aspect of her foot. She reports that the symptoms worsen with prolonged standing and improve with rest. You tap over the region just behind the medial malleolus, and the patient experiences tingling and numbness radiating into the sole of her foot. The underlying cause of her symptoms is likely related to?

explanation.text: The presentation is consistent with tarsal tunnel syndrome The underlying cause is compressive neuropathy, compression of the tibial nerve as it passes through the tarsal tunnel. Tarsal Tunnel Syndrome Definition: Compressive neuropathy of the tibial nerve at the tarsal tunnel. Symptoms Pain with prolonged standing or walking. Vague, misleading medial foot pain. Sharp, burning pain in the foot.

Numbness and intermittent paresthesias in the plantar foot. P/E Tinel’s test of the ankle is performed by tapping the tibial nerve directly over the flexor retinaculum posterior to the medial malleolus. The test is considered positive (Tinel’s sign) if the patient reports paresthesia or numbness in the distribution of the tibial nerve or its branches. (Option A, C, and D) Pain with ankle dorsiflexion and eversion.

Compression test: pain with plantar flexion and inversion, digital pressure over the tarsal tunnel (highly sensitive and specific). Investigation: Radiographs Weight-bearing radiographs to assess osseous structures. MRI Helpful to rule out accessory muscle or soft-tissue tumours. Treatment Nonoperative Lifestyle Modifications: Changes in activity to reduce symptoms. Medications: Anti-inflammatory medications. SSRIs have been used in some cases.

Bracing/Orthosis: F ootwear changes to address hindfoot alignment. Casting: Short-leg cast is an option. Operative Indications for Surgery: Failed conservative management for 3-6 months. Identified compressive mass (e.g., ganglion cyst). Positive EMG findings. Reproducible physical findings.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with difficulty wearing shoes and discomfort in her toes. She reports pain in the forefoot and has noticed that the tips of her toes frequently press into the ground while walking. On physical examination, the toes are bent at the middle and distal joints, with hyperextension at the base. The deformity worsens when wearing tight shoes. What is the most likely diagnosis based on the description of the deformity?.

explanation.text: The given image is of a claw toe, a lesser toe deformity Characterised by hyperextension of the MTP joint, along with flexion at the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints. Claw Toe Definition: Lesser toe deformity with MTP hyperextension and PIP/DIP flexion.

Diagnosis: Clinical evaluation showing: MTP hyperextension PIP flexion DIP flexion Treatment: Nonoperative Management: Shoe modifications Taping Surgical Management: Indicated for: Progressive deformity Fixed contractures Dorsal toe ulcerations Other toe deformities: (Option B, C and D)

questions.question: A 32-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a fall from a height. He complains of severe pain in the heel and inability to bear weight on his foot. On physical examination, there is swelling and tenderness at the heel. Which bone is most likely affected?.

explanation.text: The calcaneus is the largest tarsal bone located in the heel and is the most commonly fractured tarsal bone following a fall from height. Bone Group Bones Description & Function Tarsals Provide mechanical support and structure to the foot. Proximal Group Talus Transmits body weight to the foot.

Articulates at three joints: Superiorly: Ankle joint (tibia/fibula) Inferiorly: Subtalar joint (calcaneus) Anteriorly: Talonavicular joint (navicular) Calcaneus Largest tarsal bone, forms the heel. Articulates at two joints: Superiorly: Subtalar joint (talus) Anteriorly: Calcaneocuboid joint (cuboid) Intermediate Group Navicular Boat-shaped; articulates with talus, cuneiforms, and cuboid. Has a tuberosity for tibialis posterior tendon attachment.

Distal Group Cuboid Lateral; articulates with calcaneus and fourth/fifth metatarsals. Features a groove for the fibularis longus tendon. Cuneiforms (3) Medial, intermediate, lateral; wedge-shaped. Help form the transverse arch; attach to various muscles. Metatarsals I-V (1-5) Connect tarsals to phalanges; numbered medial to lateral. Have a head, neck, shaft, and base; facilitate movement and support.
Phalanges Great Toe: 2 (proximal, distal) Toes 2-5: 3 each (proximal, intermediate, distal). Each phalanx has a base, shaft, and head, providing structure to toes.

questions.question: A 35-year-old male marathon runner presents with complaints of foot pain after long-distance runs. On examination, the foot shows a well-formed arch, and palpation reveals tenderness along the medial aspect of the foot. An X-ray confirms a normal medial longitudinal arch structure. Which of the following statements incorrectly describes the function or anatomy of the medial longitudinal arch in this patient?

explanation.text: The given image is of the medial arch The medial arch is more mobile and resilient, allowing it to function effectively as a shock absorber.

Feature Medial Longitudinal Arch Lateral Longitudinal Arch Height Higher Lower Mobility More mobile, resilient Limited mobility, more rigid Shock Absorption Functions as a shock absorber(Option A rule out) Transmits weight Anterior End Heads of 1st, 2nd, 3rd metatarsals Heads of 4th, 5th metatarsals Posterior End Medial tubercle of calcaneum Lateral tubercle of calcaneum Summit Superior articular surface of the talus Articular facet on the superior surface of calcaneum (at the subtalar joint) Anterior Pillar Talus, navicular, 3 cuneiforms, 1–3 metatarsals Cuboid and 4th, 5th metatarsals Posterior Pillar Medial half of calcaneum Lateral half of calcaneum Main Joint Talocalcaneonavicular joint(Option D rule out) Calcaneocuboid joint Bony Key Stone Head of talus(Option B rule out) Cuboid Intersegmental Ties Spring ligament (Plantar calcaneo navicular ligament) Long plantar ligament, Short plantar ligament Tie Beams Medial part of plantar aponeurosis, Abductor hallucis, Medial part of flexor digitorum brevis Lateral part of plantar aponeurosis, Abductor digiti minimi, Lateral part of flexor digitorum brevis Slings Tibialis posterior, Flexor hallucis longus Peroneus longus, Peroneus brevis, Flexor digitorum longus Suspension Sling Tibialis anterior and peroneus longus Tibialis anterior and peroneus longus

questions.question: A 35-year-old patient presents with difficulty in flexing the lateral four toes. On examination, it is noted that the action of the flexor digitorum longus tendon is intact. Which of the following muscles, in the second layer of the sole, assists the flexor digitorum longus during this action?

explanation.text: The quadratus plantae in the second layer of the sole, assists the flexor digitorum longus by helping align and pull its tendon straight, thereby aiding in the flexion of the lateral four toes. First and Second layers of the sole: The abductor hallucis (Option A) (first layer) is involved in abducting the big toe.
**The flexor digitorum brevis (Option B):** (first layer) also flexes the lateral four toes but acts more proximally at the middle phalanges and does not assist the action of flexor digitorum longus.
**The lumbricals (Option D):** (second layer) are primarily involved in flexing the metatarsophalangeal joints and extending the interphalangeal joints, not in pure flexion.

questions.question: A 35-year-old male presents with a deep laceration on the posterior aspect of his knee after a road traffic accident. On surgical exploration, the popliteal artery is injured. Which of the following is not a direct branch of the popliteal artery?

explanation.text: The fibular (peroneal) artery is a branch of the posterior tibial artery, not a direct branch of the popliteal artery. Branches of the Popliteal Artery Branch Supply Muscular branches Supply the adductor magnus and hamstrings, gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris. Cutaneous branches Arise from the popliteal artery or indirectly from its muscular branches. Genicular branches: Five branches in total: two superior, two inferior, one middle.
Middle genicular artery Pierces the oblique popliteal ligament, supplies cruciate ligaments and synovial membrane of the knee.

**Medial and lateral superior genicular arteries (Option A):** Wind around the femur above the condyles, pass deep to the hamstrings. Medial and lateral inferior genicular arteries Wind around the tibial condyles, pass deep to the collateral ligaments of the knee, form anastomoses around the knee. Terminal Branches: It terminates at the lower border of popliteus by dividing into the anterior (Option C) and posterior tibial arteries (Option B)

questions.question: During a surgical procedure involving the reconstruction of the lower limb, the surgeon plans to use a perforator flap. Which of the following statements about perforating arteries is correct?

options.A: Perforating arteries are exclusively found in the thigh region.
options.B: Musculocutaneous perforators run along intermuscular septa before supplying the skin.
options.C: Perforating arteries can originate from major source arteries or adjacent vessels and are essential for flap surgery.
options.D: Septocutaneous perforators only supply the periosteum of bones.

explanation.text: Perforating arteries play a significant role in reconstructive flap surgeries as they can originate from major source arteries (e.g., femoral artery) or from vessels in adjacent tissues. This versatility is critical for ensuring adequate blood supply to the flap, which is necessary for successful healing and function.

Perforating Veins and Arteries in the Lower Limb Perforating Veins: Connecting Venous Systems Function: Essential for venous return; connect superficial veins (e.g., great and small saphenous veins) to deep veins (e.g., femoral, popliteal, tibial veins). Valve Role: Valves ensure one-way blood flow from superficial to deep veins, preventing backflow and enhancing venous return.

Classification: Direct Perforating Veins: Direct connections between superficial and deep veins. Examples: Great and Small Saphenous Veins: Major direct perforators. Small Direct Perforators: Thigh: Adductor canal perforator connects great saphenous vein to femoral vein. Below the Knee: Perforator links great saphenous vein to posterior tibial vein.

Leg: Lateral perforator joins small saphenous vein to peroneal vein; medial perforators link posterior arch vein to posterior tibial vein. Indirect Perforating Veins: Connect through muscular veins before reaching deep veins. Clinical Significance: Valve Incompetence: Faulty valves can cause varicose veins by allowing backflow from deep to superficial veins.

Post-Thrombotic Incompetence: Following DVT, perforating veins may reopen without functioning valves, leading to chronic venous insufficiency. Perforating Arteries: Blood Supply to Lower Limb Tissues Definition: Arteries that penetrate deep fascia to supply the suprafascial plexus (blood vessel network in subcutaneous tissue). Types: Direct Cutaneous Perforator: Supplies skin directly from source artery.

Periosteocutaneous Perforator: Supplies skin after traveling along a bone. Musculocutaneous Perforator: Passes through muscle before reaching the skin. Septocutaneous Perforator: Runs along an intermuscular septum to supply skin. Other Types: Include neurocutaneous, tendocutaneous, venocutaneous, and intercompartmental perforators.

Clinical Importance: Flap Surgery: Perforator flaps are used for wound coverage and reconstruction, supplied by perforating arteries. Donor Site: Lower limbs have an average of 90 perforating arteries, making them key for flap procedures.

Applications of Perforator Flaps Region Application Gluteal Region Breast reconstruction; covering sacral/perineal defects Hip and Thigh Versatile flaps from anterolateral, anteromedial thighs, TFL for various reconstructions Knee and Leg Useful for knee and lower leg defects; posterior tibial artery flaps critical for reconstructions Ankle and Foot Local skin flaps preferred due to specialized skin structure Perforating arteries are exclusively found in the thigh region (Option A): Perforating arteries are found throughout the lower limb, not exclusively in the thigh.

**Musculocutaneous perforators run along intermuscular septa before supplying the skin (Option B):** Musculocutaneous perforators pass through muscles before reaching the skin, not along intermuscular septa.
**Septocutaneous perforators only supply the periosteum of bones (Option D):** Septocutaneous perforators supply the skin after traveling along intermuscular septa.

questions.question: Which muscle is supplied by the both tibial and common peroneal nerve?

explanation.text: The biceps femoris muscle is innervated by the tibial and common peroneal nerves. The tibial nerve supplies the long head of the biceps femoris, while the common peroneal nerve supplies the short head. Therefore, the tibial and common peroneal nerves do supply the biceps femoris muscle Incorrect options: Option A: Gracilis: The gracilis muscle is primarily innervated by the obturator nerve, not the tibial or common peroneal nerve.

Therefore, the tibial and common peroneal nerves do not supply the gracilis muscle Option C: Adductor longus: The adductor longus muscle is primarily innervated by the obturator nerve, not the tibial or common peroneal nerve. Thus, the tibial and common peroneal nerves do not supply the adductor longus muscle. Option D: Adductor magnus: The adductor magnus muscle is primarily innervated by the obturator

and sciatic nerves. The sciatic nerve, which is composed of the tibial and common peroneal nerves, supplies the posterior part of the adductor magnus. However, the tibial and common peroneal nerves alone do not supply the adductor magnus muscle.

questions.question: A muscle is attached to the area marked in the given Image. What is the action of this muscle on the hip joint?

explanation.text: The muscle attached to the area marked in the given image is the gluteus maximus. The gluteus maximus is the largest muscle in the gluteal region and is primarily responsible for extending the hip joint, which means it helps to move the thigh backward. This action is commonly referred to as hip extension. Additionally, the gluteus maximus also assists in lateral rotation of the hip joint.
Lateral rotation refers to the outward rotation of the thigh away from the midline of the body.

Action of the Hip joint, corresponding muscles and their innervation: Action Muscles Nerve supply Flexion Psoas major (chief flexor) Anterior rami of L1, L2, L3 Iliacus (chief flexor) Sartorius Rectus femoris Pectineus Femoral nerve (L2, L3) Extension Gluteus maximus (chief extensor) Inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1, S2) Hamstring muscles Tibial part of the sciatic nerve (L5, S1, S2) Abduction Gluteus medius and minimus (chief abductors) Tensor fasciae latae Superior gluteal nerve (L5, S1) Adduction Adductor longus Adductor brevis Adductor magnus (chief adductors) Gracilis Obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4) Pectineus Double nerve supply (Femoral nerve and obturator nerve) Medial rotation Anterior fibres of gluteus minimus and medius (chief medial rotators) Tensor fasciae latae Superior gluteal nerve (L5, S1) Lateral rotation Piriformis Ventral rami of S1, S2 Obturator externus Posterior division of obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4) Obturator internus and Associated gemelli, Quadratus femoris (These muscles are generally termed short rotators) Nerve to obturator internus (L5, S1, S2) Flexion and medial rotation (Option A): Flexion of the hip joint involves bringing the thigh forward, towards the abdomen.

The gluteus maximus acts opposite to this motion by extending the hip, so it is not involved in hip flexion. Medial rotation refers to the inward rotation of the thigh towards the midline of the body, which is also not a primary action of the gluteus maximus.

**Adduction and lateral rotation (Option B):** Adduction involves bringing the thigh towards the midline of the body. The gluteus maximus is not directly involved in hip adduction. Lateral rotation is the correct action associated with the gluteus maximus, as explained earlier.

**Abduction and medial rotation (Option C):** Abduction refers to moving the thigh away from the midline of the body, which is not a primary action of the gluteus maximus. Medial rotation, as mentioned earlier, is not a primary action of the gluteus maximus.

questions.question: The artery that is palpated between the medial malleolus and the calcaneal tendon is?

explanation.text: The posterior tibial artery runs posterior to the medial malleolus, between the medial malleolus and the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon. It is commonly palpated at this location to assess peripheral circulation, especially in conditions like peripheral arterial disease (PAD).

Arrangement of Structures Under the Flexor Retinaculum (Medial to Lateral) Mnemonic: Tom Dick ANd Harry T: Tibialis posterior D: Flexor Digitorum longus A: Posterior tibial Artery N: Tibial Nerve H: Flexor Hallucis longus Incorrect Options: Anterior tibial artery (Option A): The anterior tibial artery is located on the anterior aspect of the leg, and it travels through the anterior compartment.
It is not palpated between the medial malleolus (inner ankle) and the calcaneal tendon (Achilles tendon).

**Dorsalis pedis artery (Option C):** The dorsalis pedis artery is located on the dorsal (top) aspect of the foot, specifically between the first and second metatarsal bones. It is not palpated between the medial malleolus and the calcaneal tendon.
**Popliteal artery (Option D):** The popliteal artery is located behind the knee joint in the popliteal fossa. It is not palpated between the medial malleolus and the calcaneal tendon.

questions.question: A patient has lost sensation over the dorsum of the foot and medial four toes. There is the associated difficulty of eversion of the foot. Which nerve injury is likely to be the reason for this?

explanation.text: The superficial peroneal nerve provides sensory innervation to the dorsum of the foot and medial four toes, except for the web space between the first and second toes (which is supplied by the deep peroneal nerve). It also supplies the lateral compartment muscles (fibularis longus and brevis), which are responsible for foot eversion.
Therefore, an injury to this nerve results in loss of sensation over the dorsum of the foot and difficulty with eversion.

Fracture of the neck of fibula → Common peroneal nerve injury Features of Common Peroneal Nerve Injury: Loss of dorsiflexion → Foot drop Complete loss of eversion No loss of complete inversion (Tibialis posterior intact via tibial nerve) Loss of extension of great toe and lateral four toes Complete sensory loss on dorsum of foot (except lateral part) Injury of Tibial Nerve Injury of Superficial Peroneal Nerve Injury of Deep Peroneal Nerve Loss of plantar flexion Eversion completely affected Loss of dorsiflexion – foot drop No loss of complete inversion (because of tibialis anterior supplied by deep peroneal nerve is intact) Loss of flexion of great toe Loss of flexion of lateral four toes Paralysis of all muscles of sole Loss of sensory supply over sole Sensory loss on major part of dorsum except medial side of foot and lateral side of foot and lateral side of little finger Inversion not completely affected because tibialis posterior functional Loss of extension of great toe Loss of extension of lateral four toes Sensory loss on the area between great and second toe Incorrect Options: Deep peroneal nerve (Option A): Supplies the anterior compartment of the leg Provides sensation only to the first web space between the first and second toes.
Injury would cause foot drop, not loss of eversion.

**Common peroneal nerve (Option C):** The common peroneal nerve branches into the superficial and deep peroneal nerves. Injury would cause a wider deficit, including foot drop (due to deep peroneal involvement) and loss of eversion and sensation over the dorsum of the foot. The given symptoms are specific to superficial peroneal nerve injury only.

**Posterior tibial nerve (Option D):** Supplies the posterior compartment of the leg. Provides sensation to the sole of the foot, not the dorsum. Injury affects plantar flexion and sensation of the sole, not eversion.

questions.question: Identify the labelled tarsal bone in the image below.

explanation.text: There are 7 tarsal bones in the foot. The Navicular is located medially in the midfoot between the talus posteriorly and the 3 cuneiform bones anteriorly. Bone Group Bones Description & Function Tarsals Provide mechanical support and structure to the foot. Proximal Group Talus Transmits body weight to the foot.

Articulates at three joints: Superiorly: Ankle joint (tibia/fibula) Inferiorly: Subtalar joint (calcaneus) Anteriorly: Talonavicular joint (navicular) Calcaneus Largest tarsal bone, forms the heel. Articulates at two joints: Superiorly: Subtalar joint (talus) Anteriorly: Calcaneocuboid joint (cuboid) Intermediate Group Navicular Boat-shaped; articulates with talus, cuneiforms, and cuboid. Has a tuberosity for tibialis posterior tendon attachment.

Distal Group Cuboid Lateral; articulates with calcaneus and fourth/fifth metatarsals. Features a groove for fibularis longus tendon. Cuneiforms (3) Medial, intermediate, lateral; wedge-shaped. Help form the transverse arch; attach to various muscles. Metatarsals I-V (1-5) Connect tarsals to phalanges; numbered medial to lateral. Have a head, neck, shaft, and base; facilitate movement and support.

Phalanges Great Toe: 2 (proximal, distal) Toes 2-5: 3 each (proximal, intermediate, distal). Each phalanx has a base, shaft, and head; provide structure to toes. Incorrect Options: Calcaneus (Option A): is the largest of the tarsal bones in the foot's heel. It bears the weight of the body as the heel touches the ground.
**Cuboid (Option B):** is the lateral bone of the foot lying in front of the calcaneus and behind the fourth and fifth metatarsal bones.
**Talus (Option D):** is the second largest tarsal bone, which lies above the calcaneus in the hindfoot.

questions.question: Abduction at the hip joint is done by

explanation.text: Abduction at the hip joint, which refers to moving the leg away from the midline of the body, is primarily performed by the gluteus medius muscle. The gluteus medius is a broad, thick muscle located on the

lateral aspect of the hip. It acts as a powerful abductor of the hip joint and plays a crucial role in maintaining stability during activities such as walking and running. Incorrect options: Option A. Gluteus maximus: The gluteus maximus is the largest muscle of the buttocks and primarily functions in extending and externally rotating the hip joint. While it can assist in abduction, it is not the primary muscle responsible for this movement.

Option C. Obturator internus: The obturator internus is a deep muscle of the hip that acts as an external rotator of the hip joint. It does not contribute significantly to hip abduction. Option D. Quadratus femoris: The quadratus femoris is a deep muscle of the hip that assists in hip joint stabilization and contributes to hip rotation. It is not a primary muscle involved in hip abduction.
